We could not establish the root cause and do not claim that every network break is gone: the Windows event log of the DEV server shows no restart of the MCP service between 22:04 UTC on 24 October and 08:43 UTC on 25 October (your session was not lost to a restart), and sandbox_call returns the API's answer, or its own error, as a tool result, never by dropping the connection. 'Transport closed' is what an MCP client reports when the connection, its session or the answer's event stream breaks between it and the server, whatever the tool did. What the server had was the most fragile transport the protocol allows: a stateful session kept in the MCP process's memory (reaped after 30 idle minutes) and every answer sent as an event stream through the TLS gateway, which also compresses it, and your VPN. From fixed_in on (compare overview's server_build with fixed_in): (1) the MCP server is stateless with plain JSON answers: each tool call is one HTTP request and its answer, with no session id to lose and no stream held open (no tool needed either). Your agent needs no change; reconnect it once after the upgrade (a new agent session). (2) sandbox_status returns recent_calls: your implementation's last 20 sandbox_call outcomes, newest first (method, path, as_user, idempotency_key, outcome, status, request_id, idempotent_replay, ms, error_type), kept per developer and implementation in the MCP service's memory (a restart empties it). outcome is answered (with the API's status and request_id), refused or failed (stopped before sending), not_sent (no connection: the API never saw the request), uncertain (sent, and the API's answer never reached the MCP server) or 'no answer recorded' (still running, or the tool call itself was cut off). A key the sandbox generates is recorded before the request is sent, so you see it in every case. (3) When the answer is lost between the MCP server and the API, sandbox_call itself answers outcome uncertain or not_sent with error_type, the elapsed ms and the original idempotency_key, instead of a bare error. Nothing is ever retried. After a transport error, read recent_calls first: answered gives you the lost answer; after uncertain or 'no answer recorded', re-read the record and follow the endpoint's write_semantics, and repeat a write only with the same idempotency_key and payload on an endpoint that takes one, exactly as you did by hand. Frontend guide 10 (the sandbox section and the tool table) says this. If an answer is lost again, report the UTC time, server_build, method and path and the recent_calls entry: it tells us whether the API answered, and we will read the gateway's and the MCP service's logs for that minute.

issues.response: Confirmed: every real source of a critical notification (a Code Red, a critical result, an overdue ER patient, an escalated incident) needs a clinical workflow and reaches every holder of a permission on the shared DEV server, so the bell's critical toast could not be accepted safely. A DEV server now lets any logged-in user send themself a real notification: POST /api/v1/notifications/test with your own access token (Idempotency-Key optional, as for any create). Every field is optional: severity critical (default), warning or info; title (shown after 'DEV test: '); body; expires_in_minutes 1-1440 (default 60); action_url (a route of your app starting with /). It answers 201 with the notification as GET /notifications lists it, plus expires_at. It is an ordinary row (category dev.test): notification.created reaches every socket of that user at once (priority critical for a critical one; the payload carries notification_id, title and severity, not the body), a reconnect with resume_from replays it, GET /notifications returns its body, the unread count includes it, and POST /notifications/{notification_id}/read marks it read. Nobody else sees it: use your own synthetic user (a demo account is shared by every developer logged in as it). Clean-up: it leaves the inbox and the unread count by itself at expires_at (notifications are never deleted). Repeat: call it again; at most ten a minute per user (429 RATE_LIMITED, details.retry_after_seconds). An agent can also send one as a demo account with sandbox_call (POST /notifications/test). It is a testing tool, not part of the contract: it is not in OpenAPI, no screen lists it, a PROD server has no such route (404), and your app must never call it. Read frontend guide 09, 'Testing the notification bell (DEV only)'. It is on the DEV server from this build on (compare overview's server_build with fixed_in).

issues.response: Confirmed: the shared DEV server is unlicensed (state dev) and locking it would lock every developer out, so nothing could test the licence screens. A DEV server now simulates grace and locked for your own requests only; nothing on the server changes and no other developer sees it. HTTP: send the header X-Haspataal-License-Simulation: grace or locked. GET /meta/license, POST /auth/login (the license in its answer) and POST /auth/refresh honour it. grace: state grace, days_left 5, logins all, login and refresh allowed. locked: state locked, logins super_admin_only; login and refresh answer 403 LICENSE_INVALID (details: state, reason, grace_until, vendor) for everyone but the Super Admin (demo.it); requests with a valid access token keep working, as on a real server. A refused refresh does not use up the refresh token. Realtime: after auth, send {"type":"simulate_license","state":"grace"} (or "locked") on your WebSocket: that socket alone receives system.license with the simulated state, "simulated": true and a negative event_id (never store it as resume_from); its topic filter applies. Restoring: stop sending the header and send {"type":"simulate_license","state":"ok"}: the socket receives system.license with the real state (dev), so your app must clear the banner. The message starts 'Simulated for DEV testing' and notice says it is a DEV simulation. A licensed (PROD) server ignores the header and the message. Not simulated: the standby states (standby_main_active, close code 1013).
